(&#8220;we,&#8221; &#8220;us,&#8221; &#8220;our,&#8221; &#8220;SunTrust,&#8221; or &#8220;the Company&#8221;) is a </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">leading provider of financial services, with our headquarters located in Atlanta, Georgia. Our principal subsidiary</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is SunTrust Bank (&#8220;the Bank&#8221;). The Company was incorporated in the State of Georgia in 1984 and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">offers a full line of financial services for consumers, businesses, corporations, institutions, and not-for-profit entities, both through its branches</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;(</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">located primarily in Florida, Georgia, Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Maryland, South Carolina, and the District of Columbia</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">) </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">and through other national delivery channels</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. The Bank offers </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">deposit, credit, and trust and investment services</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to its clients </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">through a selection of full-, self-, and assisted-service channels</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, including </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">branch, call center, Teller Connect&#8482; machines, ATMs, online, mobile, and tablet</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">.&#160;Other </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">subsidiaries provide capital markets, mortgage banking, securities brokerage, i</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;background-color:#ffffff;color:#000000;">nvestment banking, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">and wealth management services</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. At </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">December&#160;31, 2017</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, the Company had total assets of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">$206 billion</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and total style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:1px;padding-top:12px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Regulation and Supervision</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">We are limited under the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to banking, managing or controlling banks, and other activities that the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;has determined to be closely related to banking. The Company, a </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, elected to become a financial holding company pursuant to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">GLBA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, allowing it to engage in a broader range of activities that are (i) financial in nature or incidental to financial activities or (ii) complementary to a financial activity and do not pose a substantial risk to the safety and soundness of depository institutions or the financial system in general. These expanded services include securities underwriting and dealing, insurance underwriting, merchant banking, and insurance company portfolio investment, and are subject to the Volcker Rule and other restrictions discussed below.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">As a financial holding company, the Company and its banking subsidiary are required to be &#8220;well capitalized&#8221; and &#8220;well managed&#8221; while maintaining at least a &#8220;satisfactory&#8221; </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CRA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;rating. In the event of noncompliance, the Federal Reserve may, among other things, limit the Company&#8217;s ability to conduct these broader financial activities or, if the deficiencies persist, may require the Company to divest its banking subsidiary. Furthermore, if the Company does not have a satisfactory </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CRA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;rating, it may not commence any new financial activities, although the Company will still be allowed to engage in activities closely related to banking.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The Federal Reserve regulates </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s under the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, with residual supervisory authority over &#8220;functionally regulated&#8221; subsidiaries such as the Company's broker-dealer and investment </font></div></div><div style='width:2%; float:left;'>&#160;</div><div style='float:right; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">adviser subsidiaries. Our non-banking subsidiaries are regulated by various other regulatory bodies with supervisory authority over the particular activities of those subsidiaries. For example, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">STRH</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">STIS</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;are broker-dealers registered with the SEC and members of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">FINRA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">STAS</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is an investment advisor registered with the SEC. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">STIS</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is also an insurance agency registered with state insurance commissions.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The Bank is an </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">-insured commercial bank chartered under the laws of the State of Georgia and is a member of the Federal Reserve System. In addition to regulation by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, the Bank and the Company are regulated by the Georgia Department of Banking and Finance. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;also has jurisdiction over certain activities of the Bank as an insured depository institution. As a Georgia-chartered commercial bank, the Bank's powers are limited to activities permitted by Georgia and federal banking laws. Generally, the Bank may engage in all usual banking activities such as taking deposits, lending money, issuing letters of credit, currency trading, and offering safe deposit box services.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">As an umbrella supervisor under the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">GLBA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s system of functional regulation, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requires that financial holding companies operate in a safe and sound manner so that their financial condition does not threaten the viability of affiliated depository institutions. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, among other things, implemented changes that affected the oversight and supervision of financial institutions, provided for a new resolution procedure for large financial companies, created the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFPB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, introduced more stringent regulatory capital requirements and significant changes in the regulation of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">OTC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;derivatives, reformed the regulation of credit rating agencies, increased controls and transparency in corporate governance and executive compensation practices, incorporated the Volcker Rule, required registration of advisers to certain private funds, and influenced significant changes in the securitization market. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requirements typically apply to </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with greater than $10 billion of consolidated assets, and the requirements increase at certain asset size thresholds (most notably, $50 billion of consolidated assets and $250 billion of consolidated assets).</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:1px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Enhanced Prudential Standards</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with consolidated assets of $50 billion or more are subject to enhanced prudential standards and capital requirements. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;directs the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to establish heightened prudential standards for (i) risk-based capital requirements and leverage limits, (ii) liquidity risk management requirements, (iii) overall risk management requirements, (iv) stress testing, (v) resolution planning, (vi) credit exposure and concentration limits, and (vii) early remediation actions that must be taken under certain conditions in the early stages of financial distress.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In February 2014, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;adopted a final rule implementing the enhanced liquidity and risk management requirements; it requires greater supervision and oversight of liquidity and general risk management by boards of directors and includes capital planning and stress testing requirements. In </font></div></div></div><div><br></div><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:0px;padding-left:0px;padding-right:0px;padding-top:0px;text-align:center;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">1</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div><br></div><div style='display:inline-block; width:100%;'><div style='float:left; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">addition, the rule requires publicly traded U.S. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with total consolidated assets of $10 billion or more to establish enterprise-wide risk committees. The liquidity risk management requirements are in addition to those imposed by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;rule. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Enhanced Capital Standards</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:bold;">&#32;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In July 2013, the U.S. banking regulators promulgated final rules substantially implementing the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Basel III</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;capital framework and various </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;provisions (the &#8220;Capital Rules&#8221;). The Capital Rules increased regulatory capital requirements of U.S. banking organizations and revised the level at which the Bank becomes subject to corrective action as described in the &#8220;prompt corrective action&#8221; section below. The &#8220;Collins&#8221; amendment to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;required federal banking regulators to impose a generally applicable leverage capital ratio regardless of institution size and to phase out certain &#8220;hybrid&#8221; capital elements from Tier 1 capital treatment. The Company became subject to the Capital Rules on January 1, 2015. For additional information regarding the Capital Rules, including recent updates and/or changes to the rules and related requirements, refer to the "Capital Resources" section of Item 7, MD&amp;A, in this Form 10-K. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Distributions</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">There are various legal and regulatory limits on the extent to which the Bank may pay dividends or otherwise supply funds to its Parent Company. Federal and state bank regulatory agencies have the authority to prevent the Bank from paying dividends or engaging in any other activity that, in the opinion of the agency, would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice. Restrictions on capital distributions, share repurchases and redemptions, and discretionary bonus payments to executive officers are imposed on banks that are unable to sustain the capital conservation buffer above the minimum CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital ratios. The capital conservation buffer is a buffer above the minimum levels designed to ensure that banks remain well-capitalized, even in adverse economic scenarios.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">See additional discussion of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Basel III</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;in the "Capital Resources" section of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Item 7</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, MD&amp;A, in this Form 10-K.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Mandatory Liquidity Coverage Ratio (&#8220;</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#8221;); Net Stable Funding Ratio (&#8220;</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#8221;) </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In September 2014, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">OCC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, and the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;approved rulemaking that established, for the first time, a quantitative minimum </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;for large, internationally active banking organizations, and a less stringent </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;(&#8220;modified </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#8221;) for </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with less than $250 billion in total assets, such as the Company. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requires a banking entity to maintain sufficient liquidity to withstand an acute 30-day liquidity stress scenario. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;became effective for the Company on January 1, 2016, with a minimum requirement of 90% of high-quality, liquid assets to total net cash outflows; full compliance of 100% was required beginning January 1, 2017. The Company has met </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requirements within the regulatory timelines and at </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">December&#160;31, 2017</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, its </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;was above the 100% regulatory requirement.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">On </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">December&#160;19, 2016</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;published the final rule, promulgated as Regulation WW, which will require us to publicly disclose qualitative information, with certain </font></div></div><div style='width:2%; float:left;'>&#160;</div><div style='float:right; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">qualifications and permitted limitations related to information that is proprietary or confidential to the Company, about (i) certain components of our </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;calculation in a standardized tabular format (</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;disclosure template) and (ii) factors that have significant effect on the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, to facilitate an understanding of our calculations and results. The rule aims to promote market discipline by providing the public with comparable liquidity information about covered companies. The disclosures must be made on a covered company's public internet site or in a public financial or regulatory report. The disclosures must remain available to the public for at least five years from the time of initial disclosure. Covered companies subject to modified </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, including the Company, will be required to comply with disclosure requirements beginning on </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">October&#160;1, 2018</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">On </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">May&#160;3, 2016</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">OCC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, and the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;proposed a rule to implement the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. The proposal would require large U.S. banking organizations to maintain a stable funding profile over a one-year horizon. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;proposed a modified </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requirement for bank holding companies with greater than $50 billion but less than $250 billion in total consolidated assets and less than $10 billion in total on balance sheet foreign exposure. As proposed, the rule would require us to publicly disclose our </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and the components of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;each calendar quarter. The agencies intend the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to complement the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, liquidity risk management, and stress testing requirements under the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s Regulation YY (enhanced prudential standards for </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more). The proposed rule contains an implementation date of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">January&#160;1, 2018</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">; however, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">a final rule has not yet been issued</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">See additional discussion of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">LCR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">NSFR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;in the "Liquidity Risk Management" section of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Item 7</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, MD&amp;A, in this Form 10-K. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Capital Planning; Stress Testing</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Pursuant to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s are required to conduct company-run stress tests and to perform supervisory stress tests directed by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with more than $10 billion in total consolidated assets must conduct an annual company-run stress test, and those with total consolidated assets exceeding $50 billion must conduct an additional mid-cycle stress test. For company-run stress tests, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s use the same planning horizon, capital action assumptions, and scenarios as those used in the supervisory stress tests. Stress testing is designed to assess whether the covered Company's capital is sufficient to absorb losses during stressful conditions, while meeting obligations to creditors and counterparties, and, to the extent applicable, continuing to serve as credit intermediaries. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The Company also is subject to supervisory stress testing requirements under the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s Capital Plan Rule, which the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;implements as part of its </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">CCAR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;process. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">CCAR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is a broad supervisory program that includes stress testing and assesses a covered company&#8217;s practices for determining capital needs, including its risk measurement and management practices, capital planning and decision-making, and associated internal controls and governance. The Company is required to publish a summary of the results of its annual stress test, and the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;publishes the results of the stress testing under adverse and severely adverse scenarios. </font></div></div></div><div><br></div><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:0px;padding-left:0px;padding-right:0px;padding-top:0px;text-align:center;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">2</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div><br></div><div style='display:inline-block; width:100%;'><div style='float:left; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The Capital Plan Rule finalized in late 2011 requires a U.S. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;with consolidated assets of $50 billion or more to develop and maintain a capital plan that is reviewed and approved by its board of directors or a committee thereof. Capital plans are intended to allow the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to assess the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#8217;s systems and processes of incorporating forward-looking projections of assets and liabilities, revenues and losses, and to monitor and maintain their internal capital adequacy. Under the Capital Plan Rule, each capital plan must address, among other capital actions, projected capital ratios under stress scenarios, planned dividends and other capital distributions, and share repurchases over a minimum nine quarter planning horizon. Prior to executing a capital plan, a non-objection notification must be received from the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. If the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;objects to our capital plan, we may not make certain capital distributions until the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s non-objection to the distribution is received.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In January 2017, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;released a final rule that revises capital plan and stress test rules, whereby certain </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s, including the Company, with less than $250 billion in total consolidated assets will no longer be subject to the qualitative component of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#8217;s annual </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">CCAR</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. The final rule also modifies certain regulatory reports to collect additional information on nonbank assets and to reduce reporting burdens for large and noncomplex firms. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">For additional information regarding Capital Planning and Stress Testing, refer to the "Capital Resources" section of Item 7, MD&amp;A, in this Form 10-K.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Regulatory Regime for Swaps</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;established a new comprehensive regulatory regime for the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">OTC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;swaps market, aimed at increasing transparency and reducing systemic risk in the derivatives markets, including requirements for central clearing, exchange trading, capital, margin, reporting, and recordkeeping. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requires that certain swap dealers register with one or both of the SEC and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFTC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, depending on the nature of the swaps business. The Bank provisionally registered with the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFTC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;as a swaps dealer, subjecting the Bank to new requirements under this regulatory regime including trade reporting and record keeping requirements, business conduct requirements (including daily valuations, disclosure of material risks associated with swaps and disclosure of material incentives and conflicts of interest), mandatory clearing and exchange trading requirements for certain standardized swaps designated by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFTC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, and increased capital requirements established by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. Subject to the SEC's finalization of certain rules applicable to security-based swaps, the Bank expects to register with the SEC as a security-based swap dealer. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Such registration will subject the Bank&#8217;s security-based swaps business to similar </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requirements, including trade reporting, business conduct standards, recordkeeping, and potentially mandatory clearing and exchange requirements. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In 2020, our derivatives business involving uncleared swaps is expected to become subject to margin requirements established by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, which may exceed current market practice.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Resolution Planning</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s with total consolidated assets of $50 billion or more must submit resolution plans to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;addressing the </font></div></div><div style='width:2%; float:left;'>&#160;</div><div style='float:right; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">company's strategy for rapid and orderly resolution in case of material financial distress or failure. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;have widely promoted resolution plans as core elements of reforms intended to mitigate risks to the U.S. financial system, and to end the &#8220;too big to fail&#8221; status of the largest financial institutions. Covered institutions are expected to file their resolution plans annually, or at the direction of regulators, regardless of the financial condition or nature of operations of the institution. Preparation and review of these resolution plans is a major undertaking for covered financial institutions. If a plan is not credible, the Company and the Bank may be restricted in expansionary activities, or be subjected to more stringent capital, leverage, or liquidity requirements. The Company and the Bank submitted resolution plans to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;in December 2015. During 2016, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;waived the covered financial institutions' requirement to file their resolution plans. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;provided feedback regarding the Company's and the Bank's 2015 resolution plans during 2017. The Company submitted its updated resolution plan to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;in December 2017. The Bank is developing its resolution plan to be responsive to feedback received and will submit its plan to the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;in 2018.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;issued a final rule in November 2016 requiring insured depository institutions with more than two million deposit accounts to create and maintain comprehensive and detailed deposit account records to facilitate the determination of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;insured deposits in the event of a bank failure. Under the rule, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;must be able to use the failing bank's systems, data, and staff to calculate the insured and uninsured amounts for each depositor and place holds on portions of uninsured deposits. The Bank will be required to be in compliance with this rule by May 2020.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Deposit Insurance </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The Bank&#8217;s depositors are insured by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;up to the applicable limits, which is currently $250,000 per account ownership type. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;provides deposit insurance through the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">DIF</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, which the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;maintains by assessing depository institutions, including the Bank, an insurance premium. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;changed the statutory regime governing the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">DIF</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. By September 30, 2020, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;must increase the amount in the deposit insurance fund to 1.35% of insured deposits, impose a premium on banks to reach this goal, and offset the effect of assessment increases for institutions with less than $10 billion in total consolidated assets. In March 2016, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FDIC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;issued a final rule to address this surcharge on banks by collecting those premiums from banks with more than $10 billion in consolidated assets. This surcharge began in the third quarter of 2016.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Source of Strength</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;policy requires </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s to act as a source of financial strength to each subsidiary bank and to commit resources to support each subsidiary. This policy was codified in the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, though no regulations have been proposed to define the scope of this financial support.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:left;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Anti-Money Laundering (&#8220;</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#8221;), PATRIOT ACT; </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">OFAC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">&#32;Sanctions</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Anti-money laundering measures and economic sanctions have </font></div></div></div><div><br></div><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:0px;padding-left:0px;padding-right:0px;padding-top:0px;text-align:center;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">3</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div><br></div><div style='display:inline-block; width:100%;'><div style='float:left; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">long been a matter of regulatory focus in the U.S. The Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act of 1970, commonly referred to as the "Bank Secrecy Act" or "BSA," requires U.S. financial institutions to assist U.S. government agencies to detect and prevent money laundering by imposing various reporting and recordkeeping requirements on financial institutions. Passage of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">Patriot Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;renewed and expanded this focus, extending greatly the breadth and depth of anti-money laundering measures required under the BSA. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">Patriot Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requires all financial institutions to establish certain anti-money laundering compliance and due diligence programs, including enhanced due diligence policies, procedures, and controls for certain types of relationships deemed to pose heightened risks.</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;I</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">n cooperation with federal banking regulatory agencies, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network ("FinCEN") is responsible for implementing, administering, and enforcing BSA compliance.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Federal banking regulators and FinCEN continue to emphasize their expectation that financial institutions establish and implement robust BSA/</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;compliance programs. Consistent with this supervisory emphasis, in August 2014, FinCEN issued an advisory stressing its expectations for financial institutions&#8217; BSA/</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;compliance programs, including specific governance, staffing and resource allocation, and testing and monitoring requirements. Furthermore, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FinCEN proposed a rule that would require financial institutions to obtain beneficial ownership information from all legal entities with which they conduct business.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">OFAC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;has primary responsibility for administering and enforcing economic and trade sanctions, which are broad-based measures, derived from U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives. These sanctions are imposed on designated foreign countries and persons, terrorists, international narcotics traffickers, and persons involved in activities relating to proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. While the sanctions laws are separate from the BSA and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;laws, these regimes overlap in purpose. All U.S. persons must comply with U.S. sanctions laws. The Company must ensure that its operations, including its provision of services to clients, are designed to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions laws. Among other things, the Company must block accounts of, and transactions with, sanctioned persons and report blocked transactions after their occurrence.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Over the past several years, </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">federal banking regulators, FinCEN, and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">OFAC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;have increased supervisory and enforcement attention on </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">U.S.</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, as evidenced by a significant increase in enforcement activity, including several high profile enforcement actions. Several of these actions have addressed violations of </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;laws, U.S. sanctions laws, or both, resulting in the imposition of substantial civil monetary penalties. </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In both the BSA/</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and sanctions areas, enforcement actions have increasingly focused on publicly identifying individuals and holding those individuals, including compliance officers, accountable for</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;deficiencies in BSA/</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;compliance programs. State attorneys general and the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">DOJ</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;have also pursued enforcement actions against banking entities alleged to have willfully violated </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">AML</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">U.S.</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;sanctions laws. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div></div><div style='width:2%; float:left;'>&#160;</div><div style='float:right; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Consumer Financial Protection</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFPB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, established by the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, has broad rulemaking, supervisory, and enforcement powers under various federal consumer financial protection laws. Furthermore, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFPB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is authorized to engage in consumer financial education, track consumer complaints, request data, and promote the availability of financial services to under-served consumers and communities. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">CFPB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;has primary examination and enforcement authority over institutions with assets of $10 billion or more. We are subject to a number of federal and state consumer protection laws, including the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Truth in Lending Act, the Truth in Savings Act, the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, the Expedited Funds Availability Act, the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, the Fair Housing Act, the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the Service Members Civil Relief Act, and these laws&#8217; respective state-law counterparts. The Company also is subject to state laws regarding unfair and deceptive acts and practices. Violations of applicable consumer protection laws can result in significant liability from litigation brought by customers, including actual damages, restitution, and attorneys&#8217; fees. In addition, federal bank regulators, state attorneys general, and state and local consumer protection agencies may pursue remedies, such as imposition of regulatory sanctions and penalties, restrictions on expansionary activities, and requiring customer rescission rights. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Prompt Corrective Action</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The federal banking agencies have broad powers with which to require companies to take prompt corrective action to resolve problems of insured depository institutions that do not meet minimum capital requirements. The law establishes five capital categories for this purpose: (i) well-capitalized, (ii) adequately capitalized, (iii) undercapitalized, (iv) significantly undercapitalized, and (v) critically undercapitalized. The Capital Rules amended the thresholds in the prompt corrective action framework to reflect the higher capital ratios required in the Capital Rules. Under the Capital Rules, to be considered well-capitalized, an institution generally must have risk-based Total capital and Tier 1 capital ratios of at least 10% and 6%, respectively, and must not be subject to any order or written directive to meet and maintain a specific capital level for any capital measure. While the prompt corrective action rules apply to banks and not </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">s, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;is authorized to take actions at the holding company level. The banking regulatory agencies are required to take mandatory supervisory actions, and have the discretion to take other actions, as to insured depository institutions in the three undercapitalized categories, the severity of which depends on the assigned capital category. For example, an insured depository institution is generally prohibited from paying dividends or making capital distributions if it would be undercapitalized as a result. An undercapitalized institution must submit a capital restoration plan, which must be guaranteed up to certain amounts by its parent holding company. Significantly undercapitalized institutions may be subject to various requirements and restrictions, such as mandates to sell voting stock, reduce total assets, and limit or prohibit the receipt of correspondent bank deposits. Critically undercapitalized </font></div></div></div><div><br></div><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:0px;padding-left:0px;padding-right:0px;padding-top:0px;text-align:center;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">4</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div><br></div><div style='display:inline-block; width:100%;'><div style='float:left; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:13px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">institutions are subject to appointment of a receiver or conservator.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Volcker Rule</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Through the &#8220;Volcker Rule,&#8221; the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;amends the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">BHC Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;by generally prohibiting a banking entity from engaging in proprietary trading and investing in, sponsoring, or having certain other relationships with, a private equity, hedge fund, or certain other types of private funds. The term &#8220;banking entity&#8221; covers insured depository institutions, their holding companies, and certain other entities and their affiliates. There are limited exceptions to the prohibition on proprietary trading, such as trading in certain U.S. government or agency securities, engaging in certain underwriting or market-making activities, and certain hedging activities. There are also limited exceptions to the prohibitions on certain activities with covered private funds, such as for certain activities in connection with a banking entity's bona fide trust, fiduciary, or investment advisory business, as well as in connection with public welfare activities including low income housing finance. All permitted activities are subject to applicable federal or state laws, restrictions or limitations that may be imposed by the regulator, including capital and quantitative limitations as well as diversification requirements, and must not, among other things, pose a threat to the safety and soundness of the banking entity or the financial stability of the U.S. Further, the Volcker Rule's anti-evasion authority grant to the regulatory agencies requires them to impose extensive internal controls and recordkeeping requirements on banking organizations to ensure their compliance with the Volcker Rule.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Branching</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;relaxed existing interstate branching restrictions by modifying the federal statute governing de novo interstate branching by state member banks. Consequently, a state member bank may open its initial branch in a state&#160;outside of the bank&#8217;s home state by way of an interstate bank branch, so long as a bank chartered under the laws of that state would be permitted to open a branch at that location.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Restrictions on Affiliate Transactions</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">There are limits and restrictions on transactions in which the Bank and its subsidiaries may engage with the Company and other Company subsidiaries. Sections 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act and </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s Regulation W, among other things, govern terms and conditions and limit the amount of extensions of credit, and the amount of collateral required to secure extensions of credit, by the Bank and its subsidiaries to the Company and other Company subsidiaries, and limit purchases of assets by the Bank and its subsidiaries from the Company and other Company subsidiaries. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;significantly enhanced and expanded the scope and coverage of the limitations imposed by Sections 23A and 23B, specifically, by including derivative transactions as credit extensions subject to Section 23A and 23B. Furthermore, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;requires that conforming collateral be maintained for the duration of covered transactions, rather than only at the time of the transaction. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;has increased its scrutiny of Regulation W transactions, and has supported its supervision over </font></div></div><div style='width:2%; float:left;'>&#160;</div><div style='float:right; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Regulation W compliance with information received through the resolution planning process. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;has yet to amend Regulation W or provide guidance in light of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">'s changes to Sections 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Interchange Rules; &#8220;Durbin Amendment&#8221;</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">, through a provision known as the &#8220;Durbin Amendment,&#8221; required the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;to establish a cap on the interchange fees that merchants pay banks for electronic clearing of debit transactions. In 2011, the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;issued final rules that significantly limit the amount of interchange fees a bank may charge for electronic debit transactions.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Incentive Compensation</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In 2010, the FRB and other regulators jointly published final guidance for structuring incentive compensation arrangements at financial organizations. The guidance does not set forth any formulas or pay caps but contains certain principles that companies are required to follow with respect to employees and groups of employees that may expose the company to material amounts of risk. The three primary principles are (i)&#160;balanced risk-taking incentives, (ii)&#160;compatibility with effective controls and risk management, and (iii)&#160;strong corporate governance. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">FRB</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;monitors compliance with this guidance as part of its safety and soundness oversight.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;text-indent:24px;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">In 2016, the FRB, SEC, and other regulators jointly published proposed rules on incentive compensation under Section 956 of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. The proposed rules would impose several substantive requirements on the form of our incentive compensation, including (i) requiring that incentive compensation payable to a &#8220;senior executive officer&#8221; or &#8220;significant-risk taker&#8221; be subject to a 7-year clawback requirement; (ii) requiring a substantial portion of incentive compensation payable to a &#8220;senior executive officer&#8221; or &#8220;significant-risk taker&#8221; to be deferred and subject to the risk of forfeiture; (iii) prohibiting the acceleration of incentive compensation that is required to be deferred, other than in the event of death or disability; (iv) limiting the amount of incentive compensation payable to &#8220;senior executive officers&#8221; and &#8220;significant risk-takers&#8221; for the attainment of performance measures in excess of target measures (to 125% and 150% of target for &#8220;senior executive officers&#8221; and &#8220;significant risk-takers,&#8221; respectively); and (v) requiring the implementation of an independent risk-monitoring framework. In July 2017, the SEC released its rulemaking agenda and did not include the rules under Section 956 of the </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Dodd-Frank Act</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">. As a result, it is not certain when the final rules may be issued.</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;padding-top:13px;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Privacy and Cyber-Security</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">We are subject to many U.S. federal, state, and international laws and regulations governing requirements for maintaining policies and procedures to protect non-public confidential information of our customers. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">GLBA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:bold;">&#32;</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">requires us to periodically disclose our privacy policies and practices relating to sharing such information and permits consumers to opt out of our ability to share information with unaffiliated third parties under certain circumstances. Other laws and regulations, at both the federal and state level, impact our ability to share certain information </font></div></div></div><div><br></div><div style="text-align:center;"><div style="line-height:120%;padding-bottom:0px;padding-left:0px;padding-right:0px;padding-top:0px;text-align:center;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">5</font></div></div><hr style="page-break-after:always"><div><br></div><div style='display:inline-block; width:100%;'><div style='float:left; width:49%;'><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">with affiliates and non-affiliates for marketing and/or non-marketing purposes, or to contact customers with marketing offers. The </font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-weight:normal;">GLBA</font><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">&#32;also requires banking institutions to implement a comprehensive information security program that includes administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to ensure the security and confidentiality of customer records and information. These security and privacy policies and procedures, for the protection of personal and confidential information, are in effect across all businesses and geographic locations. </font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;"><br></font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;font-style:italic;font-weight:bold;">Acquisitions</font></div><div style="line-height:120%;text-align:justify;font-size:10pt;"><font style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:10pt;color:#000000;">Our ability to grow through acquisitions is limited by various regulatory approval requirements.
